title: Humour and teasing
job: Banter, irony, and when not to
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: THE DISCLAIMER IS A SENTENCE, NOT A TONE. nongdam-ieyo and jangnan-ieyo come AFTER the remark and are far less optional than English just kidding. Without one, a light remark is simply heard as a claim.

ENGLISH MARKS A JOKE WITH THE VOICE, KOREAN WITH A WORD. A learner's deadpan carries nothing across; the signal has to be said out loud. Reading the signal when it comes back at you is the other half of the skill.

-(eu)l ppeonhaesseoyo IS NOT A COUNTERFACTUAL. It says the thing did not happen and says nothing at all about what would have followed, so it never joins an if-clause. That is exactly why L4-M3 kept it out.
IT IS USUALLY HYPERBOLE. jugeul ppeonhaesseoyo, I nearly died, is comic far more often than it is literal — and here English gives a gift, because the figure is the same one, whole.
gyeou IS THE OTHER HALF OF THE PAIR. ppeonhaesseoyo says it did not happen; gyeou says it did happen, and only just. Between them they are nearly and barely, which L4-M3 could not hold together.
TEASING RUNS DOWNWARD OR SIDEWAYS. English teasing runs upward freely and reads as warmth. A Korean tease aimed at an elder is not funny in any tone of voice, and no disclaimer repairs it.
THE AMPLIFIERS A JOKE RUNS ON are jinjja, wanjeon and daebak. They are casual speech in polite clothing: right among friends and colleagues, wrong in an announcement or to an elder.
utgyeoyo IS ABOUT THE THING, useoyo ABOUT THE PERSON. A story is utgyeoyo, funny; the listener useoyo, laughs. They are one letter apart in the romanization and point in opposite directions.

sentences.cue: There's no homework today. Just kidding.

words.note: The joke itself. nongdam-ieyo, said after the remark, is what tells a listener the remark was one.

sentences.trap: English can leave a joke to the voice. Korean does not: without nongdam-ieyo the first sentence is only a claim about homework.

variations.changed: the remark with the disclaimer taken off

mistake.why: The bare noun is not the disclaimer. Korean says the whole sentence nongdam-ieyo; dropping the copula is the plain style this course does not speak.

sentences.usage: Taking back a small untruth you told for a laugh.
sentences.mnemonic: Say the joke, then say it was one.

sentences.cue: Yesterday I was so busy I nearly died.

words.note: Nearly, as a whole phrase: the verb stem takes -(eu)l and ppeonhaesseoyo follows it. A near miss, and far more often a joke about one.

sentences.trap: It says only that the thing did not happen. English I nearly died invites what would have followed; the Korean does not, and it takes no if-clause.

variations.changed: a different verb in the same frame

mistake.why: This makes it a counterfactual: if I had been busy, I would have died. ppeonhaesseoyo reports a near miss that really did nearly happen.

sentences.usage: Making a hard day sound comic.
sentences.mnemonic: Nearly — and nothing about what came next.

sentences.cue: I only just got home today.

words.note: The other half of nearly. ppeonhaesseoyo says it did not happen; gyeou says it did happen, and only just.

sentences.trap: gyeou is not nearly. A sentence with gyeou reports something that DID happen; one with ppeonhaesseoyo reports something that did not.

variations.changed: the adverb and the verb alone
gyeou moved next to the verb

mistake.why: That says I nearly came home, and therefore did not. gyeou is the word for getting there after all, with difficulty.

sentences.usage: Saying you made it, but barely.

words.cue: a story, something somebody told you
words.note: A story or an anecdote. It is what a joke usually arrives inside, and it is the ordinary word for what somebody told you.
Said of the thing, never of the person doing the laughing: a story is utgyeoyo, and the listener useoyo.

sentences.trap: utgyeoyo and useoyo are one letter apart and point opposite ways. The joke is utgyeoyo; the person who hears it useoyo.

variations.changed: the amplifier and the verb alone
the subject particle instead of the topic

mistake.why: That says the story laughs. A story is funny — utgyeoyo — and only a person useoyo.

sentences.usage: Passing on something that made you laugh.
sentences.mnemonic: The joke utgyeoyo, the listener useoyo.

sentences.display: Chingu-ga neomu utgyeoseo jeongmal manhi useoyo.
sentences.script: 친구가 너무 웃겨서 정말 많이 웃어요.
sentences.cue: My friend is so funny that I really laugh a lot.
sentences.literal: friend-SUBJ too is-funny-BECAUSE really a-lot laugh

words.note: What a person does. Its past useosseoyo already belongs to L4-M10, so this row teaches the present and the -aseo form only.

sentences.trap: -aseo hangs off the stem. utgyeoyo becomes utgyeoseo and useoyo becomes useoseo; neither of them keeps its -yo.
sentences.sound: CHIN-gu-ga NEO-mu UT-gyeo-seo JEONG-mal MA-ni U-seo-yo.

variations.cue: It's so funny that I laugh a lot.

mistake.display: Chingu-ga neomu useoseo jeongmal manhi utgyeoyo.
mistake.script: 친구가 너무 웃어서 정말 많이 웃겨요.
mistake.why: The two verbs have swapped places. It now says the friend laughs so much that I am the funny one.

sentences.usage: Explaining why somebody had you in stitches.

words.note: A one-word reaction to something remarkable, good or bad. It is exclamation rather than description, so it usually stands on its own.
An amplifier in front of a verb or an adjective. Stronger than L3-M1's jeongmal, and lighter in tone.

sentences.trap: All three amplifiers are casual speech in polite clothing. They fit friends and colleagues, and they do not fit an announcement or an elder.

mistake.why: daebak on its own is the plain style. In the -yo speech this course writes, the reaction still carries the copula: daebak-ieyo.

sentences.usage: Reacting to a story you enjoyed.

sentences.cue: My friend is really good fun.

words.note: The everyday amplifier, and a whole question on its own: jinjja means really? L3-M1's jeongmal is its more careful twin.
Built from jaemi, fun, and isseoyo, and written as one word. Said of a person it means good company, not that they tell jokes.

sentences.trap: jaemiisseoyo about a person means good company. utgyeoyo about a person would say they are ridiculous, so the two are not interchangeable.

variations.changed: the past, said of a story

mistake.why: jaemiisseoyo is written as one word. Split in two it reads as a bare noun and a separate verb, which is not how the phrase is said.

sentences.mnemonic: jaemi and isseoyo, written as one.

sentences.cue: There's an exam today, you know. I'm only teasing.

words.note: The test itself. Korean often leaves the particle off after it in speech, which is why it stands bare in sihum itjanayo.

sentences.trap: L4-M4's -janayo assumes the listener already knows. That is what makes it a tease: it presents an invention as common knowledge.

mistake.why: Without jangnan-ieyo the tease is just a false statement, and the listener has no way to hear it as anything else. The disclaimer is not decoration.

sentences.usage: Winding a friend up and then letting them off.

sentences.cue: You must not tease an elder.

words.note: The act rather than the words. jangnan-ieyo withdraws a tease the way nongdam-ieyo withdraws a joke.

sentences.trap: English teasing runs upward and reads as warmth. Korean teasing runs downward or sideways, and no tone of voice makes it acceptable upward.

variations.cue: You must not joke with an elder.
variations.changed: a joke rather than a tease, the same rule

mistake.why: Grammatical and still wrong. The second half of this module is that a tease chooses its listener before it chooses its words.

sentences.usage: Naming the one place a tease does not go.

words.note: The noun inside jaemiisseoyo. The verdict on a flat joke is jaemi-ga eopseoyo, and it is milder in Korean than it sounds translated.

sentences.trap: A flat joke gets no harsher verdict than this. jaemi-ga eopseoyo is the ordinary thing to say, not the insult that isn't funny sounds like in English.

variations.changed: a story rather than a joke

mistake.why: The particle is doing work: jaemi-ga is the subject of eopseoyo. Fast speech drops it, but the phrase a learner writes carries it.

sentences.usage: Telling a friend their joke fell flat.

comprehensionPool.cue: There's no exam today. Just kidding.
You must not joke with an elder.
